Bayesian neural nets

Variational inference · PyTorch

Bayes by Backprop

From a line with error bars to a neural network that knows what it doesn’t know — derived end to end, every symbol defined before it is used.

Contents

Use Contents above or the ☰ menu (top) to jump to a section; inside a section, the In this section links jump to its subsections. Prev / Next or the ← → arrow keys page through.

Jargon, in plain words

Bayesian inference
updating beliefs with data using Bayes’ rule: posterior ∝ likelihood × prior. The output is a distribution, not a single answer.
Prior / posterior
belief before / after seeing the data.
Likelihood
how well a particular setting of the weights explains the observed data.
Evidence
the probability of the data averaged over all weight settings; the hard-to-compute normaliser that forces the approximations below.
Variational inference
replacing an intractable posterior with the closest member of a simple family of distributions, found by optimisation.
Stochastic variational inference
variational inference carried out by stochastic gradient ascent on the ELBO — each step uses a cheap, noisy, unbiased gradient estimate. The framework this whole page lives in.
Mean-field
the simplifying assumption that the approximate posterior factorises — one independent distribution per weight, ignoring correlations.
ELBO
evidence lower bound: the quantity variational inference maximises; it equals the log-evidence minus the gap to the true posterior.
KL divergence
a directed “distance” between two distributions; appears both as the thing we minimise and as the complexity penalty in the loss.
Reparameterisation trick
writing a random weight as a deterministic function of its parameters plus fixed noise, so gradients can flow through the sampling step.
Monte Carlo
estimating an average by drawing random samples and averaging them.
Minibatch
a small random subset of the data used to estimate a gradient cheaply, instead of the whole dataset.
Score-function vs reparameterisation gradient
two ways to get a stochastic gradient of an expectation: the score-function (REINFORCE) estimator works for any \(q\) but is noisy; the reparameterisation (pathwise) estimator needs a reparameterisable \(q\) and is far less noisy. This page uses the second.
Epistemic uncertainty
uncertainty from not having enough data; it shrinks as data grows. This is the part that fans the band out.
Aleatoric uncertainty
irreducible noise in the measurements themselves; it does not shrink with more data.
MAP estimate
maximum a posteriori: the single most probable weight setting — a Bayesian method collapsed back to one number.
Laplace approximation
approximating a posterior by a Gaussian centred at its peak (the MAP), with covariance taken from the curvature there. The quickest stand-in for variational inference (used in the Bridge).
Logistic sigmoid
the S-shaped function \(\sigma(z)=1/(1+e^{-z})\) that maps any real score to a probability in \((0,1)\).
Bernoulli likelihood
the probability model for a single yes/no outcome; its product over the data points is the likelihood in logistic regression and in a classification BNN.
Calibration
whether the error bars are honest: a 90% interval should contain the truth about 90% of the time.
HMC
Hamiltonian Monte Carlo: a gold-standard sampler that draws from the exact posterior, more accurate but costlier than variational inference.
Collocation points
(Part III) locations where a PDE is enforced on the network, needing no measured data — the physics acts as extra “observations”.

Part IThe simplest example: Bayesian linear regression

In this section

Before any network, start with a straight line fitted the Bayesian way. Everything important — priors, posteriors, a predictive band that grows away from the data — is already here, and here it can be solved exactly, with no approximation and no training loop. The neural network in Part II is this same idea with the exact solution swapped for a learned one.

The model

We fit \(y=w_0+w_1x\). Collect the two weights into \(\mathbf w=(w_0,w_1)\) and write each input as a two-entry row \(\boldsymbol\phi(x)=(1,\ x)\), so the line is the dot product \(f_{\mathbf w}(x)=\boldsymbol\phi(x)\,\mathbf w\). Stacking all \(N\) rows gives the design matrix \(\boldsymbol\Phi\) (size \(N\times 2\)). With Gaussian noise,

\[ y_n=\boldsymbol\phi(x_n)\,\mathbf w+\varepsilon_n,\qquad \varepsilon_n\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma_n^2),\qquad \beta\equiv\frac1{\sigma_n^2}. \]

Here \(\beta\) (the likelihood precision) is just the inverse noise variance — precision is the Bayesian habit of measuring certainty as one-over-variance. We place a zero-mean Gaussian prior on the weights with prior precision \(\alpha\):

\[ p(\mathbf w)=\mathcal N\!\big(\mathbf w\mid \mathbf 0,\ \alpha^{-1}\mathbf I\big). \]

The posterior, in closed form

Because a Gaussian prior and a Gaussian likelihood combine into a Gaussian posterior, Bayes’ rule can be done with algebra instead of sampling. The posterior over the weights is \(p(\mathbf w\mid\mathcal D)=\mathcal N(\mathbf w\mid \mathbf m_N,\ \mathbf S_N)\) with

\[ \mathbf S_N^{-1}=\alpha\mathbf I+\beta\,\boldsymbol\Phi^{\!\top}\boldsymbol\Phi,\qquad \mathbf m_N=\beta\,\mathbf S_N\,\boldsymbol\Phi^{\!\top}\mathbf y. \]

In words: \(\mathbf S_N\) is the posterior covariance (how uncertain the weights are) and \(\mathbf m_N\) is the posterior mean (the best-fit line). More data, or less noise (larger \(\beta\)), makes \(\mathbf S_N^{-1}\) larger and so the posterior tighter.

The predictive band

To predict at a new \(x_\star\) we average the line over the whole posterior. The result is again Gaussian, with

\[ \text{mean}=\boldsymbol\phi(x_\star)\,\mathbf m_N,\qquad \underbrace{\operatorname{Var}[y_\star]}_{\text{total}}=\underbrace{\tfrac1\beta}_{\text{aleatoric}}+\underbrace{\boldsymbol\phi(x_\star)\,\mathbf S_N\,\boldsymbol\phi(x_\star)^{\!\top}}_{\text{epistemic}}. \]

The two pieces are exactly the split we will meet again: a fixed noise floor \(1/\beta\), plus a term that grows as \(x_\star\) moves away from the data, because there the posterior over the slope and intercept disagree most.

in code → S = inv(alpha*I + beta·ΦᵀΦ), m = beta·S·Φᵀy; the band is 1/beta + einsum(Φ,S,Φ). Full script below.
blr.py — exact Bayesian linear regressionclick to expand 
"""Warm-up: exact Bayesian linear regression (closed form). Produces blr_uncertainty.png."""
import numpy as np
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

np.random.seed(1)

# True line y = a + b x, observed with Gaussian noise, data clustered on the right.
a_true, b_true, noise = 0.3, 0.8, 0.25
x = np.concatenate([np.random.uniform(0.2, 1.2, 8), np.random.uniform(2.6, 3.4, 6)])
y = a_true + b_true * x + noise * np.random.randn(x.size)

# Design matrix with columns [1, x].
Phi = np.stack([np.ones_like(x), x], axis=1)           # (N, 2)

alpha = 0.5                 # prior precision: w ~ N(0, alpha^-1 I)
beta = 1.0 / noise**2       # likelihood precision = 1/noise^2

# Closed-form Gaussian posterior over weights:
S_inv = alpha * np.eye(2) + beta * Phi.T @ Phi         # posterior precision
S = np.linalg.inv(S_inv)                               # posterior covariance
m = beta * S @ Phi.T @ y                               # posterior mean

# Predictive distribution on a grid.
xs = np.linspace(-1.0, 4.5, 200)
Phis = np.stack([np.ones_like(xs), xs], axis=1)
pred_mean = Phis @ m
pred_var = 1.0 / beta + np.einsum("ij,jk,ik->i", Phis, S, Phis)   # aleatoric + epistemic
pred_std = np.sqrt(pred_var)

# A few lines sampled from the posterior over weights.
samples = np.random.multivariate_normal(m, S, size=12)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5))
for w in samples:
    ax.plot(xs, w[0] + w[1] * xs, color="#4c72b0", alpha=0.18, lw=1)
ax.fill_between(xs, pred_mean - 2 * pred_std, pred_mean + 2 * pred_std,
                color="#4c72b0", alpha=0.18, label="predictive ±2σ")
ax.plot(xs, pred_mean, color="#2f4a7c", lw=2, label="posterior mean")
ax.plot(xs, a_true + b_true * xs, "k--", lw=1.1, label="true line")
ax.scatter(x, y, s=22, color="#c44e52", zorder=5, label="data")
ax.set_xlabel("x"); ax.set_ylabel("y")
ax.set_title("Bayesian linear regression: the band is narrowest where the data sits")
ax.legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=8)
fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig("blr_uncertainty.png", dpi=130)
print("saved blr_uncertainty.png")

BridgeBayesian logistic regression

In this section

Change the output of Part I from a number to a yes/no and the same Bayesian recipe gives you calibrated probabilities — but the tidy closed form disappears. This is the simplest useful model whose posterior has no exact form, so it is the first time we must approximate it. That approximation is the whole subject of the Interlude and of the neural network in Part II; here we meet its cheapest version on a model simple enough to see every step.

The model

The output is binary, \(y\in\{0,1\}\). We pass the same linear score \(\mathbf w^\top\boldsymbol\phi(x)\) through the logistic sigmoid \(\sigma\) to turn it into a probability, and model the label as a coin flip with that bias:

\[ \sigma(z)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-z}},\qquad p(y=1\mid x,\mathbf w)=\sigma\!\big(\mathbf w^\top\boldsymbol\phi(x)\big). \]

With a Gaussian prior \(p(\mathbf w)=\mathcal N(\mathbf 0,\Sigma_p)\), the likelihood over the data is a product of Bernoulli terms \(\prod_n \sigma_n^{\,y_n}(1-\sigma_n)^{1-y_n}\), writing \(\sigma_n=\sigma(\mathbf w^\top\boldsymbol\phi(x_n))\).

Why the closed form breaks

In Part I a Gaussian prior times a Gaussian likelihood gave a Gaussian posterior, solved with algebra. Here the likelihood is Bernoulli, not Gaussian, and a Gaussian prior times a Bernoulli likelihood is not any standard distribution: the posterior \(p(\mathbf w\mid\mathcal D)\) has no closed form and its normaliser is an intractable integral. There is nothing to solve exactly — we must approximate, which is exactly the situation the neural network faces, one layer deeper.

The Laplace approximation

The cheapest approximation fits a Gaussian to the posterior at its peak. First find the most probable weights (the MAP estimate) by maximising the log-posterior — a convex problem, a few Newton steps:

\[ \hat{\mathbf w}=\arg\max_{\mathbf w}\ \sum_{n}\Big[y_n\log\sigma_n+(1-y_n)\log(1-\sigma_n)\Big]-\tfrac12\mathbf w^\top\Sigma_p^{-1}\mathbf w. \]

Then approximate the posterior by a Gaussian centred there, with covariance set by the curvature — the Hessian \(\mathbf H\) of the negative log-posterior at \(\hat{\mathbf w}\):

\[ q(\mathbf w)=\mathcal N\!\big(\hat{\mathbf w},\,\mathbf H^{-1}\big),\qquad \mathbf H=\boldsymbol\Phi^\top\mathbf S\,\boldsymbol\Phi+\Sigma_p^{-1},\quad \mathbf S=\mathrm{diag}\big(\sigma_n(1-\sigma_n)\big). \]
in code → Newton's method finds w and the Hessian H; the Laplace covariance is cov = inv(H).

The predictive, pulled toward 0.5

To predict at \(x_\star\) we average the sigmoid over that Gaussian. The integral has no exact form either, but a one-line probit approximation is excellent: with latent mean \(\mu_a=\hat{\mathbf w}^\top\boldsymbol\phi(x_\star)\) and variance \(\sigma_a^2=\boldsymbol\phi(x_\star)^\top\mathbf H^{-1}\boldsymbol\phi(x_\star)\),

\[ p(y=1\mid x_\star,\mathcal D)\approx\sigma\!\left(\frac{\mu_a}{\sqrt{1+\pi\sigma_a^2/8}}\right). \]

The effect is the point of the whole page, now in probability space: where the weights are uncertain (\(\sigma_a^2\) large), the factor shrinks the score toward zero and the probability toward \(0.5\) — the model says “I don't know” rather than committing. A plug-in that just uses \(\hat{\mathbf w}\) skips this and is overconfident.

in code → p_pred is the probit-squashed average, p_map the overconfident plug-in; the band comes from sampling weights from q.
blogit.py — Bayesian logistic regression (Laplace)click to expand 
"""Bridge: Bayesian logistic regression via the Laplace approximation.
Produces blogit_uncertainty.png. The first model with no closed-form posterior."""
import numpy as np
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

np.random.seed(2)

# 1-D binary data: P(y=1) rises with x, with data in two clusters and a gap.
x = np.concatenate([np.random.uniform(-3.0, -1.0, 22),
                    np.random.uniform(1.0, 3.0, 22)])
p_true = 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-2.5 * x))
y = (np.random.rand(x.size) < p_true).astype(float)

Phi = np.stack([np.ones_like(x), x], axis=1)          # design matrix [1, x]
Sig_p_inv = (1.0 / 9.0) * np.eye(2)                   # Gaussian prior N(0, 9 I)

# --- MAP by Newton's method (log-posterior is concave: a convex optimisation) ---
w = np.zeros(2)
for _ in range(100):
    p = 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-(Phi @ w)))
    grad = Phi.T @ (p - y) + Sig_p_inv @ w
    S = p * (1.0 - p)
    H = (Phi * S[:, None]).T @ Phi + Sig_p_inv        # Hessian of neg log-posterior
    w = w - np.linalg.solve(H, grad)

cov = np.linalg.inv(H)                                # Laplace covariance = H^{-1}

# --- predictive on a grid ---
xs = np.linspace(-6, 6, 300)
Phis = np.stack([np.ones_like(xs), xs], axis=1)
mu_a = Phis @ w                                       # latent mean
var_a = np.einsum("ij,jk,ik->i", Phis, cov, Phis)     # latent variance

kappa = 1.0 / np.sqrt(1.0 + np.pi * var_a / 8.0)      # probit "squash" factor
p_pred = 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-kappa * mu_a))          # posterior-averaged probability
p_map = 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-mu_a))                   # plug-in MAP probability

# credible band by sampling weights from the Laplace posterior
W = np.random.multivariate_normal(w, cov, 500)
P = 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-(W @ Phis.T)))
lo, hi = np.percentile(P, [2.5, 97.5], axis=0)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5))
ax.fill_between(xs, lo, hi, color="#4c72b0", alpha=0.18, label="95% credible band")
ax.plot(xs, p_pred, color="#2f4a7c", lw=2.2, label="posterior-averaged P(y=1)")
ax.plot(xs, p_map, "--", color="#c44e52", lw=1.6, label="plug-in MAP (overconfident)")
ax.scatter(x, y, s=26, color="#c44e52", zorder=5, edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.5, label="data (0/1)")
ax.axvspan(-1.0, 1.0, color="grey", alpha=0.08)
ax.axhline(0.5, color="grey", lw=0.8, ls=":")
ax.text(0, 0.56, "no data here\n→ pulled toward 0.5", ha="center", fontsize=9, color="grey")
ax.set_xlabel("x"); ax.set_ylabel("P(y = 1)"); ax.set_ylim(-0.05, 1.05)
ax.set_title("Bayesian logistic regression: honest probabilities, not overconfident ones")
ax.legend(loc="center left", fontsize=8)
fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig("blogit_uncertainty.png", dpi=130)
print("saved blogit_uncertainty.png")

How this connects. Laplace is the quick cousin of the variational inference in the Interlude — both replace an intractable posterior with a Gaussian, one by curvature at the peak, the other by optimisation. And logistic regression is literally a one-unit neural network with a sigmoid output: give it hidden layers and fit it with stochastic variational inference instead of Laplace, and you have the Bayesian neural network of Part II.

Part IIThe Bayesian neural network

In this section

Swap the straight line \(\boldsymbol\phi(x)\,\mathbf w\) for a neural network \(f_{\mathbf w}(x)\) and the closed-form posterior vanishes — the evidence integral is no longer a Gaussian. The rest of this part is one standard way to recover an approximate posterior anyway.

1 · Model and posterior

Same noise model as before, now with a network in place of the line:

\[ y_n = f_{\mathbf{w}}(x_n) + \varepsilon_n, \qquad \varepsilon_n \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_n^{2}). \] \[ p(\mathbf{w}\mid\mathcal{D}) = \frac{p(\mathcal{D}\mid\mathbf{w})\,p(\mathbf{w})}{p(\mathcal{D})}, \qquad p(\mathcal{D})=\int p(\mathcal{D}\mid\mathbf{w})\,p(\mathbf{w})\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{w}. \]

That integral runs over every weight in the network, so it cannot be computed. Everything below dodges it.

2 · A variational approximation

Replace the true posterior with a simple family \(q_{\boldsymbol\theta}(\mathbf w)\) and tune \(\boldsymbol\theta\) to bring it as close as possible. The mean-field Gaussian uses one independent Gaussian per weight:

\[ q_{\boldsymbol\theta}(\mathbf{w}) = \prod_{i} \mathcal{N}\!\big(w_i \mid \mu_i,\ \sigma_i^{2}\big),\qquad \sigma_i=\operatorname{softplus}(\rho_i)=\log(1+e^{\rho_i}). \]

The softplus keeps \(\sigma_i>0\) while \(\rho_i\) ranges freely, so ordinary gradient descent can’t push the spread negative.

in code → w_mu is \(\mu\), w_rho is \(\rho\), F.softplus(w_rho) is \(\sigma\), inside BayesLinear.

3a · First, what \(\mathbb{E}_q[\cdot]\) means

The expectation \(\mathbb{E}_q[g(\mathbf w)]\) is just a probability-weighted average of a quantity \(g\): go over every possible weight value, weight each by how likely \(q\) says it is, and add up. When \(q\) is spread over a handful of discrete values it is a plain sum. Suppose a single weight \(w\) could be \(1,2,3\) with probabilities \(0.2,0.5,0.3\), and some per-weight loss takes the values \(g(1)=4,\ g(2)=1,\ g(3)=5\). Then

\[ \mathbb{E}_q[g] = 0.2\cdot4 + 0.5\cdot1 + 0.3\cdot5 = 2.8. \]

For a continuous Gaussian \(q=\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2)\) the sum becomes an integral, but the two cases we need are elementary: \(\mathbb{E}_q[w]=\mu\) and \(\mathbb{E}_q[w^2]=\mu^2+\sigma^2\). When \(g\) has no closed form — our network’s log-likelihood — we use the definition directly and estimate the average by sampling:

\[ \mathbb{E}_q\big[g(\mathbf w)\big] \;\approx\; \frac1S\sum_{s=1}^{S} g\big(\mathbf w^{(s)}\big),\qquad \mathbf w^{(s)}\sim q. \]

That Monte-Carlo average is exactly what the training loop computes: draw \(S\) weight sets, evaluate the loss on each, average. So “\(\mathbb{E}_q[\cdot]\)” in the equations and “average over a few sampled networks” in the code are the same thing.

3b · The objective: the ELBO

Closeness to the posterior is measured by \(\mathrm{KL}\big(q_{\boldsymbol\theta}(\mathbf w)\,\|\,p(\mathbf w\mid\mathcal D)\big)\). Expanding it and using \(p(\mathbf w\mid\mathcal D)=p(\mathcal D,\mathbf w)/p(\mathcal D)\) splits the constant log-evidence into two movable pieces:

\[ \underbrace{\log p(\mathcal{D})}_{\text{constant}} = \underbrace{\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol\theta)}_{\text{ELBO}} + \mathrm{KL}\big(q_{\boldsymbol\theta}(\mathbf{w})\,\|\,p(\mathbf{w}\mid\mathcal{D})\big). \]

The left side is fixed and the KL is \(\ge 0\), so maximising the ELBO minimises the gap to the true posterior. The ELBO is a fit term minus a prior term, and the loss we minimise is its negative:

\[ \boxed{\;\mathcal{F}(\boldsymbol\theta) = \underbrace{-\,\mathbb{E}_{q_{\boldsymbol\theta}}\!\big[\log p(\mathcal{D}\mid\mathbf{w})\big]}_{\text{data fit}} + \underbrace{\mathrm{KL}\big(q_{\boldsymbol\theta}(\mathbf{w})\,\|\,p(\mathbf{w})\big)}_{\text{complexity}}\;} \]

3c · The data-fit term

With Gaussian noise the log-likelihood is a scaled sum of squared errors:

\[ \log p(\mathcal{D}\mid\mathbf{w}) = \sum_{n=1}^{N}\log\mathcal{N}\!\big(y_n\mid f_{\mathbf{w}}(x_n),\sigma_n^{2}\big) = -\sum_{n=1}^{N}\!\left[\frac{\big(y_n-f_{\mathbf{w}}(x_n)\big)^{2}}{2\sigma_n^{2}} + \tfrac12\log\!\big(2\pi\sigma_n^{2}\big)\right]. \]

3d · The complexity term

For two Gaussians the KL is closed-form, so nothing is sampled here. With prior \(p(w_i)=\mathcal N(0,\sigma_p^2)\), summed over every weight:

\[ \mathrm{KL}\big(q\,\|\,p\big) = \sum_{i}\left[\log\frac{\sigma_p}{\sigma_i} + \frac{\sigma_i^{2}+\mu_i^{2}}{2\sigma_p^{2}} - \tfrac12\right]. \]
in code → _kl_term(mu, sigma) is this bracket, summed; prior_sigma is \(\sigma_p\).

3e · A worked ELBO, on real numbers

Take the smallest non-trivial case: one weight \(w\), one data point \((x,y)=(1,2)\), observation noise \(\sigma_n=1\), prior \(p(w)=\mathcal N(0,1)\) so \(\sigma_p=1\). For a candidate \(q=\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2)\) both terms are elementary. Using \(\mathbb{E}_q[(y-wx)^2]=(y-\mu x)^2+\sigma^2 x^2\) from the rules above,

\[ \mathbb{E}_q[\log p(\mathcal D\mid w)] = -\tfrac12\big[(2-\mu)^2+\sigma^2+\log 2\pi\big],\qquad \mathrm{KL}(q\,\|\,\text{prior}) = -\log\sigma + \tfrac{\sigma^2+\mu^2}{2} - \tfrac12. \]

Try \(q=\mathcal N(1,\,0.5^2)\): the fit term is \(-1.544\), the KL is \(0.818\), so the ELBO is \(\mathcal L=-2.362\). Now use the exact posterior, which for this conjugate problem is \(\mathcal N(1,\,0.5)\) — mean \(1\), variance \(\tfrac12\), i.e. \(\sigma=\sqrt{0.5}\approx0.707\): the fit term is \(-1.669\), the KL is \(0.597\), and \(\mathcal L=-2.266\). The second \(q\) scores higher, and that number is exactly the log-evidence

\[ \log p(\mathcal D) = \log\mathcal N\!\big(y\mid 0,\ \sigma_n^2+\sigma_p^2\big) = \log\mathcal N(2\mid 0,2) = -2.266. \]

So the ELBO reaches its ceiling precisely when \(q\) equals the true posterior; the shortfall at any other \(q\) is the KL between \(q\) and that posterior. Maximising the ELBO and getting close to the posterior are, by construction, the same job.

elbo_fig.py — the worked ELBO exampleclick to expand 
"""ELBO worked example: one weight, one data point. Shows ELBO <= log-evidence,
with equality at the true posterior. Produces elbo_demo.png."""
import numpy as np
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

x, y, sn, sp = 1.0, 2.0, 1.0, 1.0          # data (x,y), noise std, prior std

def elbo(mu, sig):
    Eloglik = -0.5 * ((y - mu*x)**2/sn**2 + sig**2*x**2/sn**2 + np.log(2*np.pi*sn**2))
    kl = -np.log(sig/sp) + (sig**2 + mu**2)/(2*sp**2) - 0.5
    return Eloglik - kl

# Exact posterior (conjugate Gaussian) and exact log-evidence.
var = 1.0/(1/sp**2 + x**2/sn**2);  mu_post = var*(x*y/sn**2);  sig_post = var**0.5
v = sn**2 + x**2*sp**2
logZ = -0.5*(y**2/v + np.log(2*np.pi*v))

BLUE, RED, CEIL = "#3f5c93", "#c44e52", "#5c6470"
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 4))

mus = np.linspace(-1, 3, 200)
ax[0].plot(mus, [elbo(m, sig_post) for m in mus], color=BLUE, lw=2)
ax[0].axhline(logZ, ls="--", color=CEIL, lw=1.2, label=f"log evidence = {logZ:.3f}")
ax[0].axvline(mu_post, ls=":", color=RED, lw=1.2)
ax[0].scatter([mu_post], [elbo(mu_post, sig_post)], color=RED, zorder=5, label=f"optimum μ={mu_post:.2f}")
ax[0].set_xlabel("posterior mean μ  (σ fixed at optimum)"); ax[0].set_ylabel("ELBO")
ax[0].legend(fontsize=8, loc="lower center")

sigs = np.linspace(0.15, 2.0, 200)
ax[1].plot(sigs, [elbo(mu_post, s) for s in sigs], color=BLUE, lw=2)
ax[1].axhline(logZ, ls="--", color=CEIL, lw=1.2, label=f"log evidence = {logZ:.3f}")
ax[1].axvline(sig_post, ls=":", color=RED, lw=1.2)
ax[1].scatter([sig_post], [elbo(mu_post, sig_post)], color=RED, zorder=5, label=f"optimum σ={sig_post:.2f}")
ax[1].set_xlabel("posterior spread σ  (μ fixed at optimum)"); ax[1].set_ylabel("ELBO")
ax[1].legend(fontsize=8, loc="lower center")

fig.suptitle("The ELBO is a lower bound on the log-evidence, tight at the true posterior")
fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig("elbo_demo.png", dpi=130)
print("saved elbo_demo.png")

4 · Reparameterisation and the gradient

The data-fit term is an expectation over \(q_{\boldsymbol\theta}\), and we need its gradient with respect to the parameters that define \(q\). The reparameterisation trick moves the randomness into a parameter-free \(\boldsymbol\varepsilon\):

\[ \mathbf{w} = \boldsymbol\mu + \boldsymbol\sigma \odot \boldsymbol\varepsilon,\qquad \boldsymbol\varepsilon\sim\mathcal N(\mathbf 0,\mathbf I). \] \[ \nabla_{\boldsymbol\theta}\,\mathbb{E}_{q}\!\big[\log p(\mathcal D\mid\mathbf w)\big] = \mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol\varepsilon}\!\big[\nabla_{\boldsymbol\theta}\log p(\mathcal D\mid \boldsymbol\mu+\boldsymbol\sigma\odot\boldsymbol\varepsilon)\big] \approx \frac{1}{S}\sum_{s=1}^{S}\nabla_{\boldsymbol\theta}\log p\big(\mathcal D\mid \mathbf w^{(s)}\big). \]
in code → w = w_mu + w_sigma * torch.randn_like(w_sigma) is one draw; the loop averages n_samp \(=S\) draws per step.

5 · The training loop

  • Sample. A forward pass draws fresh \(\mathbf w^{(s)}=\boldsymbol\mu+\boldsymbol\sigma\odot\boldsymbol\varepsilon\) and caches its per-layer KL.
  • Score. Accumulate the Gaussian negative log-likelihood over \(S\) draws and add the one closed-form KL: \(\mathcal F=\mathrm{NLL}+\mathrm{KL}\).
  • Step. loss.backward() then opt.step() update \(\boldsymbol\mu\) and \(\boldsymbol\rho\) with Adam.

A weight the data pins down is driven to small \(\sigma_i\); one the data barely touches keeps its prior-sized \(\sigma_i\), because the KL only rewards shrinking \(\sigma\) when the likelihood doesn’t object. That surviving spread becomes the band.

6 · The predictive distribution

Predict by integrating the likelihood against the (approximate) posterior:

\[ p(y_\star\mid x_\star,\mathcal D) = \int p(y_\star\mid x_\star,\mathbf w)\,p(\mathbf w\mid\mathcal D)\,\mathrm d\mathbf w \approx \frac1S\sum_{s=1}^{S}p\big(y_\star\mid x_\star,\mathbf w^{(s)}\big),\quad \mathbf w^{(s)}\sim q_{\boldsymbol\theta}. \]

Run the trained net \(S\) times at \(x_\star\) and summarise. The mean is the prediction; the variance splits into the same two sources as in Part I:

\[ \underbrace{\operatorname{Var}\!\big[y_\star\big]}_{\text{total}} \approx \underbrace{\frac1S\sum_{s=1}^{S}\big(f_{\mathbf w^{(s)}}(x_\star)-\bar f\big)^{2}}_{\text{epistemic (model)}} + \underbrace{\sigma_n^{2}}_{\text{aleatoric (noise)}},\qquad \bar f=\frac1S\sum_s f_{\mathbf w^{(s)}}(x_\star). \]
in code → samples.std(0) is the epistemic root-variance; combined with noise_std in quadrature for the band.

7 · Reading the picture

Over the data clusters the sampled curves agree, the epistemic term collapses, and the band narrows to roughly \(\pm 2\sigma_n\). In the gap and past the last points the weights are underdetermined, the curves diverge, and the band opens up — the curved version of Part I’s bowtie. A deterministic network draws one confident line through the gap with no warning; this “knowing what it doesn’t know” is what makes Bayesian nets useful for Bayesian optimisation and active learning.

Honest caveats. The mean-field factorisation ignores correlations between weights and typically underestimates uncertainty; the noise \(\sigma_n\) is fixed here, for stability. Natural next steps: MC-dropout (cheaper), a Laplace approximation around the MAP, or full HMC/NUTS for the untruncated posterior — and in 1-D a Gaussian process is the gold-standard benchmark.

Classification BNNs

Everything above used a Gaussian likelihood for a real-valued target. To classify instead, change only the last layer and the likelihood: pass the final output through a sigmoid (binary) or softmax (multi-class), and swap the Gaussian negative log-likelihood for the Bernoulli or categorical cross-entropy — exactly the Bridge's likelihood, now sitting on top of hidden layers. For binary labels,

\[ p(y=1\mid x,\mathbf w)=\sigma\!\big(f_{\mathbf w}(x)\big),\qquad -\log p(\mathcal D\mid\mathbf w)=-\sum_n\big[y_n\log\sigma_n+(1-y_n)\log(1-\sigma_n)\big]. \]

The reparameterisation trick, the KL term and the whole SVI training loop are unchanged. Predictions are the average of the class probabilities over sampled networks, and the uncertainty now shows up as probabilities pulled toward uniform (toward \(0.5\) for binary) wherever the sampled networks disagree — the Bridge's “pulled toward 0.5” effect, now with a flexible, curved decision boundary instead of a single sigmoid.

8 · The code

About 120 lines, self-contained; the symbols above map one-to-one onto it. It writes bnn_uncertainty.png, the figure at the top.

$ pip install torch matplotlib numpy
$ python bnn_simple.py
bnn_simple.py — Bayes by Backpropclick to expand 
r"""
A very simple Bayesian Neural Network (BNN) — 1-D regression.
=============================================================

Idea in one line
----------------
An ordinary neural net learns ONE value for each weight. A Bayesian neural
net instead learns a *distribution* over each weight. Predictions are then
made by averaging over many weight samples, which gives us not just a mean
prediction but an honest estimate of how *uncertain* that prediction is.

We train with "Bayes by Backprop" (Blundell et al., 2015), which is just
variational inference done with ordinary gradient descent:

    - Approximate the (intractable) posterior over weights q(w) by a
      fully-factorised Gaussian:  w ~ N(mu, sigma^2).
    - Learn mu and sigma by maximising the ELBO, i.e. minimising
          loss = E_q[ -log p(data | w) ]  +  KL( q(w) || prior(w) ).
    - The reparameterisation trick  w = mu + sigma * eps  (eps ~ N(0,1))
      lets gradients flow through the sampling step.

The payoff is visible in the figure: where we have data the predictive band
is tight; where we have NO data (the gap in the middle, and off the edges)
the band fans out — the model says "I don't know here", which a standard
net cannot do.
"""
import math
import numpy as np
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

torch.manual_seed(0)
np.random.seed(0)

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Toy data:  y = sin(2x) + noise, with a deliberate GAP in the middle
#    so we can see uncertainty grow where there is nothing to learn from.
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
def f_true(x):
    return np.sin(3.0 * x)                                        # gentle ~1 cycle over [-1.5, 1.5]

def make_data(n=60, noise=0.06):
    x = np.concatenate([np.linspace(-1.3, -0.4, n // 2),
                        np.linspace(0.4, 1.3, n // 2)])           # gap in [-0.4, 0.4]
    y = f_true(x) + noise * np.random.randn(x.size)
    return (torch.tensor(x, dtype=torch.float32).unsqueeze(1),
            torch.tensor(y, dtype=torch.float32).unsqueeze(1))

X, Y = make_data()


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. A Bayesian linear layer.
#    Each weight has a learnable mean (mu) and a learnable spread.
#    We store the spread as "rho" and map it through softplus so that
#    sigma = log(1 + exp(rho)) is always positive.
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
class BayesLinear(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, n_in, n_out, prior_sigma=3.0):
        super().__init__()
        self.prior_sigma = prior_sigma
        # Variational parameters for weights and biases:
        self.w_mu  = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(n_out, n_in) * 0.1)
        self.w_rho = nn.Parameter(torch.full((n_out, n_in), -3.0))   # start near-deterministic
        self.b_mu  = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(n_out))
        self.b_rho = nn.Parameter(torch.full((n_out,), -3.0))

    def forward(self, x):
        # Draw one sample of the weights via the reparameterisation trick.
        w_sigma = F.softplus(self.w_rho)
        b_sigma = F.softplus(self.b_rho)
        w = self.w_mu + w_sigma * torch.randn_like(w_sigma)
        b = self.b_mu + b_sigma * torch.randn_like(b_sigma)
        self._kl = self._kl_term(self.w_mu, w_sigma) + self._kl_term(self.b_mu, b_sigma)
        return F.linear(x, w, b)

    def _kl_term(self, mu, sigma):
        # Analytic KL between q=N(mu,sigma^2) and prior=N(0, prior_sigma^2),
        # summed over every weight in this layer.
        p = self.prior_sigma
        return (torch.log(torch.tensor(p)) - torch.log(sigma)
                + (sigma ** 2 + mu ** 2) / (2 * p ** 2) - 0.5).sum()


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. The network: two Bayesian layers with a tanh in between.
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
class BNN(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, hidden=64):
        super().__init__()
        self.l1 = BayesLinear(1, hidden)
        self.l2 = BayesLinear(hidden, 1)
        self.noise_std = 0.1            # assumed observation noise (fixed, for simplicity)

    def forward(self, x):
        h = torch.tanh(self.l1(x))
        return self.l2(h)

    def kl(self):
        return self.l1._kl + self.l2._kl


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Train by minimising the negative ELBO.
#    negative ELBO = (Gaussian negative log-likelihood of the data)
#                    + KL(posterior || prior) / N_data
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
model = BNN()
opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-2)
N = X.shape[0]

for step in range(8000):
    opt.zero_grad()
    # Average a few weight samples per step for a lower-variance gradient:
    nll = 0.0
    n_samp = 3
    noise_var = model.noise_std ** 2
    for _ in range(n_samp):
        pred = model(X)                  # fresh weight sample per forward pass
        nll = nll + 0.5 * (((Y - pred) ** 2) / noise_var
                           + math.log(2 * math.pi * noise_var)).sum()
    nll = nll / n_samp
    # Full-dataset ELBO: total data likelihood + one full KL to the prior.
    loss = nll + model.kl()
    loss.backward()
    opt.step()
    if step % 2000 == 0:
        print(f"step {step:4d}   loss {loss.item():8.2f}", flush=True)


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Predict: because every forward pass samples fresh weights, we just
#    run the net many times and look at the spread of the outputs.
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
xs = torch.linspace(-1.5, 1.5, 300).unsqueeze(1)
with torch.no_grad():
    samples = torch.stack([model(xs) for _ in range(300)]).squeeze(-1)  # (300 draws, 300 points)
mean = samples.mean(0).numpy()
epistemic = samples.std(0).numpy()                    # uncertainty from the weights
std = np.sqrt(epistemic ** 2 + model.noise_std ** 2)  # + observation noise = total predictive std
xs_np = xs.squeeze(1).numpy()

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# 6. Plot: data, posterior mean, and ±2 std predictive band.
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5))
truth = f_true(xs_np)
ax.plot(xs_np, truth, "k--", lw=1.2, label="true function")
ax.fill_between(xs_np, mean - 2 * std, mean + 2 * std,
                color="#4c72b0", alpha=0.25, label="predictive ±2σ")
ax.plot(xs_np, mean, color="#4c72b0", lw=2, label="posterior mean")
ax.scatter(X.numpy(), Y.numpy(), s=18, color="#c44e52", zorder=5, label="training data")
ax.axvspan(-0.4, 0.4, color="grey", alpha=0.08)
ax.text(0, ax.get_ylim()[0] + 0.1, "no data here\n→ uncertainty grows",
        ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=9, color="grey")
ax.set_xlabel("x"); ax.set_ylabel("y")
ax.set_title("Bayesian neural network: tight where it has seen data, uncertain where it hasn't")
ax.legend(loc="upper right", fontsize=8)
fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig("bnn_uncertainty.png", dpi=130)
print("saved bnn_uncertainty.png", flush=True)

InterludeWhere this all sits: stochastic variational inference

In this section

Everything in Part II is one instance of stochastic variational inference (SVI). The name is just three ideas we have already met, bolted together:

  • Variational — approximate the intractable posterior with a tractable family \(q_{\boldsymbol\theta}\) and tune \(\boldsymbol\theta\) (§2).
  • Inference — the target is the posterior over the unknowns; here, the network weights.
  • Stochastic — we climb the ELBO by stochastic gradient ascent: every step uses a cheap, noisy, but unbiased estimate of the gradient rather than the exact one.

That third word is the engine, and the ELBO gradient picks up its noise from two independent places:

  1. Sampling the weights. The expectation \(\mathbb{E}_q[\cdot]\) in the data-fit term is estimated with \(S\) Monte-Carlo draws via the reparameterisation trick (§4). That is one source of randomness in every gradient.
  2. Subsampling the data. The sum over all \(N\) points can itself be estimated from a random minibatch \(\mathcal B\), rescaled so the estimate stays unbiased. That is the second source.

Put both together and the loss we actually differentiate each step is the stochastic estimate

\[ \widehat{\mathcal F} = -\,\frac{N}{|\mathcal B|}\sum_{n\in\mathcal B}\ \frac1S\sum_{s=1}^{S}\log p\big(y_n\mid f_{\mathbf w^{(s)}}(x_n)\big)\;+\;\mathrm{KL}\big(q_{\boldsymbol\theta}\,\|\,p\big),\qquad \mathbf w^{(s)}=\boldsymbol\mu+\boldsymbol\sigma\odot\boldsymbol\varepsilon^{(s)}. \]

The factor \(N/|\mathcal B|\) scales the minibatch sum back up to full-data size, so \(\widehat{\mathcal F}\) is an unbiased estimate of the true loss \(\mathcal F\); the KL is a sum over weights, not data, so it is computed in full every step. Feed \(\widehat{\mathcal F}\) to Adam and you are doing SVI. Our training loop is simply the full-batch case, \(|\mathcal B|=N\) with \(S\) small; at survey scale (billions of galaxies in the photo-z example) the minibatch factor is what makes the same recipe run at all.

How each part of this page relates

SVI across the page
sectionrelation to SVI
Part I — Bayesian linear regressionconjugate, so the posterior is exact in closed form — SVI is unnecessary here. It is precisely the answer SVI would converge to.
Bridge — Bayesian logistic regressionnon-conjugate; here approximated by Laplace (a Gaussian at the MAP) — the quick alternative to the SVI used from Part II on.
Part II — the BNNnon-conjugate, so we must approximate: SVI with the reparameterisation gradient. “Bayes by Backprop” is this exact combination.
Interlude — herethe general recipe; Part II is its full-batch special case.
Part III — B-PINNSVI again (one of two standard routes), with the PDE-residual term added to each minibatch’s likelihood; HMC is the non-variational alternative.
Part IV — cosmologythe same SVI recipe, where minibatching is essential at survey scale and calibrated error bars are the whole point.

The family tree

Classical VI dates to the 1990s for conjugate models. SVI (Hoffman et al., 2013) added stochastic optimisation so it could scale to huge datasets. The remaining question — how to get the stochastic gradient of \(\mathbb{E}_q[\cdot]\) when the model is not conjugate — has two standard answers, and the reparameterisation one is what this page uses.

Variational inferenceclosest simple \(q\), by optimisation
Stochastic VI (SVI)maximise the ELBO by stochastic gradient ascent
Score-function / BBVIREINFORCE gradient; any \(q\), higher variance
ADVIreparameterisation + autodiff; automatic
Bayes by Backpropreparameterisation over NN weights — this page
in code → our loop is full-batch SVI: the n_samp draws are the \(S\) Monte-Carlo samples; to make it minibatched SVI, sum the likelihood over a random batch and multiply by N/len(batch).

Part IIIFrom BNN to Bayesian PINN

A physics-informed neural network (PINN) adds the governing differential equation to the loss: the residual of the PDE is penalised at a cloud of collocation points, so the network is pulled toward solutions that obey the physics even where no data exists. A Bayesian PINN (B-PINN) does this inside the framework above — a prior over weights, and a likelihood with two parts: one for the noisy measurements and one for the PDE residual. The predictive band then reflects uncertainty from sparse data and from the physics constraint.

Part IVIn cosmology

In this section

Bayesian neural networks matter in cosmology for the same reason as everywhere else: a parameter estimate without a trustworthy error bar is not a measurement. They have been used to map observations (CMB maps, density fields, galaxy images) to cosmological parameters while reporting calibrated uncertainty, and to flag when a model is extrapolating beyond its training distribution. Below are two small worked examples in that spirit, then a reading list.

These two demos are synthetic and illustrative. They are a few lines of fake data built to show the behaviour the real pipelines are designed for — calibrated, data-driven error bars — not reproductions of them. The real studies are cited in IV.3.

IV.1 · Worked example: photometric redshifts (photo-z)

A galaxy’s brightness in a few broad filters (for LSST: \(u,g,r,i,z,y\)) is cheap to measure for billions of objects, but its redshift is what cosmology needs. As redshift grows, the 4000 Å spectral break slides to redder bands, so a galaxy’s colours (differences between filter magnitudes) encode \(z\). Inferring \(z\) from colours is photometric redshift estimation, and honest error bars are essential: the mapping is noisy, and faint galaxies have noisier colours.

The demo fakes three colours as smooth functions of \(z\), trains the Bayes-by-Backprop regressor from Part II on a bright sample (clean colours, as a spectroscopic training set would be), and tests across all brightness — the real spec-z/photo-z mismatch. The result is the behaviour these BNNs are prized for:

why it matters → a photo-z catalogue with calibrated per-object uncertainty lets a weak-lensing or clustering analysis down-weight the galaxies it can’t trust, instead of being biased by them.
photoz_demo.py — synthetic photo-z BNNclick to expand 
r"""
Worked example: photometric redshift (photo-z) with a Bayesian neural network.
==============================================================================
Illustrative SYNTHETIC demo in the spirit of LSST photo-z BNNs (Jones et al. 2023).

Real photo-z: a galaxy's brightness in a few broad filters (LSST: u,g,r,i,z,y)
is measured, and we infer its redshift z. The 4000 Angstrom break shifts to
redder bands as z grows, so galaxy *colours* (magnitude differences between
bands) encode z. Two complications make honest error bars essential:
  - colour-redshift DEGENERACY: different z can give near-identical colours,
  - FAINT galaxies have noisier photometry, hence noisier colours.
A BNN reports larger predictive uncertainty exactly in those regimes.

Here we fake 3 colours as smooth, partly-degenerate functions of z, add
magnitude-dependent noise, and train a small Bayes-by-Backprop regressor.
"""
import math, numpy as np, torch, torch.nn as nn, torch.nn.functional as F
torch.manual_seed(0); np.random.seed(0)

# ---- synthetic catalogue: z -> 3 colours, with a degeneracy and faint-end noise ----
def simulate(n):
    z = np.random.uniform(0.0, 1.5, n)
    bright = np.random.uniform(0, 1, n)                 # 1 = bright, 0 = faint
    # colours: smooth in z, but c2 is non-monotonic -> two z map to similar colours
    c1 = 1.2*z + 0.1*np.sin(6*z)
    c2 = 0.9*np.sin(2.2*z) + 0.3*z                      # degenerate (non-monotonic)
    c3 = 0.7*z**1.3
    noise = 0.03 + 0.35*(1 - bright)**1.5               # faint galaxies: much bigger noise
    C = np.stack([c1, c2, c3], 1) + noise[:, None]*np.random.randn(n, 3)
    return C.astype("float32"), z.astype("float32")[:, None], bright

# Realistic photo-z setup: the spectroscopic TRAINING sample is BRIGHT and clean;
# the photometric TEST sample spans bright -> faint. Faint test galaxies have noisy
# colours that fall outside the training manifold, so the BNN's epistemic
# uncertainty genuinely grows for them -- exactly the behaviour we want.
Cf, Zf, Bf = simulate(4000)
train = Bf > 0.55                                        # bright, well-measured subset
Xtr, Ytr = Cf[train], Zf[train]
Xte, Yte, bte = simulate(500)
mx, sx = Xtr.mean(0), Xtr.std(0)
Xtr = (Xtr - mx)/sx; Xte = (Xte - mx)/sx
Xtr, Ytr, Xte = map(torch.tensor, (Xtr, Ytr, Xte))

# ---- compact Bayes-by-Backprop layers (same idea as bnn_simple.py) ----
class BayesLinear(nn.Module):
    def __init__(s, ni, no, ps=1.0):
        super().__init__(); s.ps = ps
        s.w_mu = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(no, ni)*0.1); s.w_rho = nn.Parameter(torch.full((no, ni), -3.0))
        s.b_mu = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(no));          s.b_rho = nn.Parameter(torch.full((no,), -3.0))
    def forward(s, x):
        ws, bs = F.softplus(s.w_rho), F.softplus(s.b_rho)
        w = s.w_mu + ws*torch.randn_like(ws); b = s.b_mu + bs*torch.randn_like(bs)
        s._kl = s._kl1(s.w_mu, ws) + s._kl1(s.b_mu, bs)
        return F.linear(x, w, b)
    def _kl1(s, mu, sig):
        p = s.ps
        return (math.log(p) - torch.log(sig) + (sig**2 + mu**2)/(2*p**2) - 0.5).sum()

class PhotoZBNN(nn.Module):
    def __init__(s, h=48):
        super().__init__(); s.l1 = BayesLinear(3, h); s.l2 = BayesLinear(h, h); s.l3 = BayesLinear(h, 1)
        s.noise_std = 0.05
    def forward(s, x): return s.l3(torch.tanh(s.l2(torch.tanh(s.l1(x)))))
    def kl(s): return s.l1._kl + s.l2._kl + s.l3._kl

model = PhotoZBNN(); opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), 5e-3); N = Xtr.shape[0]
for step in range(3000):
    opt.zero_grad(); nv = model.noise_std**2
    nll = sum(0.5*(((Ytr - model(Xtr))**2)/nv + math.log(2*math.pi*nv)).sum() for _ in range(2))/2
    (nll + model.kl()).backward(); opt.step()
    if step % 1000 == 0: print(f"step {step} loss {(nll+model.kl()).item():.1f}", flush=True)

# ---- predictive mean and uncertainty on the test set ----
with torch.no_grad():
    S = torch.stack([model(Xte) for _ in range(300)]).squeeze(-1).numpy()   # (300, Nte)
zmean = S.mean(0); zstd = np.sqrt(S.std(0)**2 + model.noise_std**2)
ztrue = Yte.squeeze(1)

import matplotlib; matplotlib.use("Agg"); import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.2, 4.2))
sc = ax[0].errorbar(ztrue, zmean, yerr=2*zstd, fmt="o", ms=3, lw=.6, alpha=.5,
                    color="#3f5c93", ecolor="#9db4d8", capsize=0)
ax[0].plot([0, 1.5], [0, 1.5], "k--", lw=1)
ax[0].set_xlabel("true redshift  z"); ax[0].set_ylabel("predicted  z  (±2σ)")
ax[0].set_title("Photo-z: prediction vs truth")

ax[1].scatter(bte, zstd, s=9, color="#c44e52", alpha=.35)
bins = np.linspace(0, 1, 9); mids = 0.5*(bins[:-1]+bins[1:])
med = [np.median(zstd[(bte >= bins[i]) & (bte < bins[i+1])]) for i in range(len(bins)-1)]
ax[1].plot(mids, med, "-o", color="#7a1d30", lw=2, ms=4, label="binned median")
ax[1].set_xlabel("galaxy brightness  (1 = bright, 0 = faint)")
ax[1].set_ylabel("predictive σ(z)")
ax[1].set_title("Error bars grow for faint galaxies"); ax[1].legend(fontsize=8)
fig.tight_layout(); fig.savefig("photoz_demo.png", dpi=130); print("saved photoz_demo.png")

IV.2 · Worked example: a screened modified-gravity parameter

Many alternatives to General Relativity (for instance \(f(R)\) gravity) add a fifth force that boosts the growth of cosmic structure, set by a strength parameter — call it \(f_{R0}\). The catch is screening: in dense regions and as \(f_{R0}\to0\) the fifth force is suppressed and the signal collapses onto the standard \(\Lambda\)CDM baseline. There the data cannot constrain \(f_{R0}\) at all, and an honest model must say so with a wide error bar rather than a confident guess.

The demo fakes a clustering summary that is flat in \(f_{R0}\) near zero (screened) and only responds for larger values, then regresses \(f_{R0}\) with the same BNN:

why it matters → here the error bar itself carries physics. A confident small \(f_{R0}\) would be a false detection of standard gravity; the widening band says “consistent with GR, but not actually measured.”
modgrav_demo.py — synthetic modified-gravity BNNclick to expand 
r"""
Worked example: inferring a modified-gravity parameter with a Bayesian NN.
=========================================================================
Illustrative SYNTHETIC demo in the spirit of "Bayesian deep learning for
cosmic volumes with modified gravity" (A&A 2024, arXiv:2309.00612).

Modified-gravity (MG) models (e.g. f(R)) add a fifth force that boosts the
growth of cosmic structure, controlled by a strength parameter we call
f_R0 (larger = more deviation from General Relativity). Crucially, SCREENING
suppresses the fifth force in dense regions and for small f_R0: as f_R0 -> 0
the MG signal vanishes into the LambdaCDM baseline, so the data stop
constraining it. An honest model must report LARGE uncertainty there, rather
than a confident (and meaningless) estimate.

Here we fake a single clustering summary statistic s(f_R0) that saturates to
the GR value as f_R0 -> 0 (screening) and only responds for larger f_R0,
plus observational scatter. A BNN regresses f_R0 from s and reports error
bars that blow up in the screened regime -- the physically correct behaviour.
"""
import math, numpy as np, torch, torch.nn as nn, torch.nn.functional as F
torch.manual_seed(0); np.random.seed(0)

# ---- synthetic: f_R0 in [0, 1] (arb. units) -> clustering boost that screens near 0 ----
def simulate(n):
    fR0 = np.random.uniform(0.0, 1.0, n)
    # signal is GENUINELY FLAT near fR0=0 (screening): slope -> 0, so small fR0
    # becomes unconstrainable from the data -> uncertainty must blow up there.
    signal = 1.0 - np.exp(-4.0*fR0**2)       # quadratic (flat) at 0, rises, saturates
    s = signal + 0.05*np.random.randn(n)     # observational scatter
    return s.astype("float32")[:, None], fR0.astype("float32")[:, None]

Xtr, Ytr = simulate(1600); Xte, Yte = simulate(400)
mx, sx = Xtr.mean(), Xtr.std()
Xtr = torch.tensor((Xtr-mx)/sx); Xte = torch.tensor((Xte-mx)/sx); Ytr = torch.tensor(Ytr)

class BayesLinear(nn.Module):
    def __init__(s, ni, no, ps=1.0):
        super().__init__(); s.ps = ps
        s.w_mu = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(no, ni)*0.1); s.w_rho = nn.Parameter(torch.full((no, ni), -3.0))
        s.b_mu = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(no));          s.b_rho = nn.Parameter(torch.full((no,), -3.0))
    def forward(s, x):
        ws, bs = F.softplus(s.w_rho), F.softplus(s.b_rho)
        w = s.w_mu + ws*torch.randn_like(ws); b = s.b_mu + bs*torch.randn_like(bs)
        s._kl = s._kl1(s.w_mu, ws) + s._kl1(s.b_mu, bs)
        return F.linear(x, w, b)
    def _kl1(s, mu, sig):
        p = s.ps; return (math.log(p) - torch.log(sig) + (sig**2+mu**2)/(2*p**2) - 0.5).sum()

class MGBNN(nn.Module):
    def __init__(s, h=40):
        super().__init__(); s.l1 = BayesLinear(1, h); s.l2 = BayesLinear(h, 1); s.noise_std = 0.05
    def forward(s, x): return s.l2(torch.tanh(s.l1(x)))
    def kl(s): return s.l1._kl + s.l2._kl

model = MGBNN(); opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), 1e-2)
for step in range(5000):
    opt.zero_grad(); nv = model.noise_std**2
    nll = sum(0.5*(((Ytr-model(Xtr))**2)/nv + math.log(2*math.pi*nv)).sum() for _ in range(2))/2
    (nll + model.kl()).backward(); opt.step()
    if step % 2000 == 0: print(f"step {step} loss {(nll+model.kl()).item():.1f}", flush=True)

with torch.no_grad():
    S = torch.stack([model(Xte) for _ in range(300)]).squeeze(-1).numpy()
pm = S.mean(0); ps = np.sqrt(S.std(0)**2 + model.noise_std**2); yt = Yte.squeeze(1)

import matplotlib; matplotlib.use("Agg"); import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.2, 4.2))
o = np.argsort(yt)
ax[0].fill_between(yt[o], (pm-2*ps)[o], (pm+2*ps)[o], color="#4c72b0", alpha=.2, label="±2σ")
ax[0].scatter(yt, pm, s=9, color="#3f5c93", alpha=.6, label="predicted")
ax[0].plot([0, 1], [0, 1], "k--", lw=1, label="truth")
ax[0].axvspan(0, 0.25, color="grey", alpha=.10)
ax[0].text(0.12, 0.9, "screened\nregime", ha="center", fontsize=8, color="grey")
ax[0].set_xlabel(r"true MG strength  $f_{R0}$"); ax[0].set_ylabel(r"predicted  $f_{R0}$")
ax[0].set_title("MG parameter: prediction vs truth"); ax[0].legend(fontsize=8, loc="lower right")

ax[1].scatter(yt, ps, s=10, color="#c44e52", alpha=.6)
ax[1].axvspan(0, 0.25, color="grey", alpha=.10)
ax[1].set_xlabel(r"true MG strength  $f_{R0}$"); ax[1].set_ylabel(r"predictive σ($f_{R0}$)")
ax[1].set_title("Uncertainty blows up where gravity is screened")
fig.tight_layout(); fig.savefig("modgrav_demo.png", dpi=130); print("saved modgrav_demo.png")

IV.3 · Further reading

  1. lensingL. Perreault-Levasseur, Y. Hezaveh & R. Wechsler, “Uncertainties in Parameters Estimated with Neural Networks: Application to Strong Gravitational Lensing,” ApJL 850 (2017) L7. OSTI — an early, influential use of dropout-based BNNs for parameter errors.
  2. CMBH. J. Hortúa et al., “Parameter estimation for the cosmic microwave background with Bayesian neural networks,” Phys. Rev. D 102 (2020) 103509. APS
  3. N-bodyH. J. Hortúa et al., “Constraining cosmological parameters from N-body simulations with Variational Bayesian Neural Networks,” 2023. preprint
  4. photo-zE. Jones et al., “Improving Photometric Redshift Estimation for Cosmology with LSST using Bayesian Neural Networks,” 2023. arXiv:2306.13179
  5. mod. gravity“Bayesian deep learning for cosmic volumes with modified gravity,” A&A (2024). arXiv:2309.00612
  6. listG. Stein, ml-in-cosmology: a curated index of machine-learning-in-cosmology papers. GitHub

A note on method. Much of modern cosmological inference also uses simulation-based inference (likelihood-free inference) and normalising flows, which target the posterior over physical parameters directly rather than over network weights. They are complementary to the weight-space BNNs derived here; a future section could contrast the two.

Appendix · Notation

Every symbol used on this page, collected for reference. Each is also defined in prose where it first appears.

Data and model
symbolmeaning
\(x,\ y\)a single input and its observed (scalar) output.
\(N\)the number of training points.
\(\mathcal{D}\)the dataset, \(\mathcal D=\{(x_n,y_n)\}_{n=1}^N\).
\(\mathbf{w}\)all the model’s weights (and biases) stacked into one vector; \(w_i\) is the \(i\)-th entry.
\(f_{\mathbf w}(x)\)the model’s output at \(x\) when its weights are \(\mathbf w\) (a line in Part I, a network in Part II).
\(\varepsilon_n\)the observation noise on point \(n\): the random scatter of a measurement around the true value.
\(\sigma_n\)the standard deviation of that noise; \(\sigma_n^2\) its variance.
\(x_\star,\ y_\star\)a new test input and the prediction we want there.
Probability
symbolmeaning
\(\mathcal{N}(\cdot\mid m,v)\)a Gaussian (normal) distribution with mean \(m\) and variance \(v\).
\(p(\mathbf w)\)prior: what we believe about the weights before seeing data.
\(p(\mathcal D\mid\mathbf w)\)likelihood: how probable the data is for a given set of weights.
\(p(\mathbf w\mid\mathcal D)\)posterior: belief about the weights after seeing the data.
\(p(\mathcal D)\)evidence (or marginal likelihood): the normalising constant; an integral over all weights.
\(\mathbb{E}_{q}[\cdot]\)the average (expected value) of a quantity when weights are drawn from the distribution \(q\).
\(\mathrm{KL}(q\,\|\,p)\)the Kullback–Leibler divergence: a non-negative measure of how far \(q\) is from \(p\) (zero only when equal).
\(\odot\)element-wise (component-by-component) multiplication of two vectors.
The variational approximation (Part II)
symbolmeaning
\(q_{\boldsymbol\theta}(\mathbf w)\)a simple, tractable stand-in for the posterior, with tunable parameters \(\boldsymbol\theta\).
\(\boldsymbol\theta\)the set \(\{\mu_i,\sigma_i\}\) of all the means and spreads we actually learn.
\(\mu_i,\ \sigma_i\)the mean and standard deviation of the Gaussian over weight \(w_i\).
\(\rho_i\)an unconstrained parameter that produces \(\sigma_i=\operatorname{softplus}(\rho_i)>0\).
\(\sigma_p\)the standard deviation of the prior on each weight, \(p(w_i)=\mathcal N(0,\sigma_p^2)\).
\(\boldsymbol\varepsilon\)parameter-free noise \(\sim\mathcal N(\mathbf 0,\mathbf I)\) used to sample weights (reparameterisation).
\(S\)the number of Monte-Carlo weight samples averaged per step.
\(\mathcal L,\ \mathcal F\)the ELBO (to maximise) and the loss \(\mathcal F=-\mathcal L\) (to minimise).
\(\mathcal B,\ |\mathcal B|\)a random minibatch of data points and its size (used in SVI, below).
Bayesian logistic regression (Bridge)
symbolmeaning
\(\sigma(z)\)the logistic sigmoid \(1/(1+e^{-z})\), mapping a score to a probability.
\(\boldsymbol\phi(x)\)the feature (design) row for input \(x\) — here \((1,\ x)\).
\(\Sigma_p\)the covariance of the Gaussian prior on the weights.
\(\hat{\mathbf w}\)the MAP (most probable) weights.
\(\mathbf H\)the Hessian of the negative log-posterior at \(\hat{\mathbf w}\); \(\mathbf H^{-1}\) is the Laplace covariance.
